### Round goal

Port grok ``xai-codebase-graph``'s tree-sitter bridge free functions to Python -- the parse front of direction (2). This round lands ``range_for_node`` (grok ``Range::for_tree_node`` range.rs L170-L189), ``scope_graph_from_definitions_query`` (graph.rs L485-L556), ``extract_symbols_fast`` (graph.rs L565-L633) and ``build_scope_graph`` (mod.rs L30-L38). These are the only functions in the crate that touch tree-sitter, and they are the兑现点 (payoff point) of the deferred-binding promise R300 (range.py L9-L14) + R303 (types.py L11-L24) made when the lower leaves were kept stdlib-clean: this is the *only* module that imports ``tree_sitter``, and it does so lazily behind a ``RuntimeError`` guard. With R305e the ``scope_graph`` subpackage reaches functional parity with grok's parse path -- the remaining direction-(2) work (``manager/`` cache layer, ``index_manager.rs``, ``navigation.rs``) consumes this bridge but adds no new tree-sitter surface.

### Fusion conclusion

Functional-clone, NOT line-clone -- the methodology held for the entire R300-R305e arc. Five load-bearing decisions. First, **no ``tree_sitter`` PyPI hard dependency** -- the bridge ``import tree_sitter`` lazily inside ``_new_query_cursor`` and raises ``RuntimeError`` (NOT ``ImportError``) on absence, so callers see the same "bridge needs the binding" signal R303's ``TSLanguageConfig.language()`` / ``compile_query()`` emit; the lower 8 leaves (range/types/interner/languages/scope_graph runtime) stay zero-dependency and importable without tree-sitter installed. Second, **duck-typed, not bound** -- grok reaches tree-sitter through ``node.range()`` / ``node.byte_range()`` / ``query.capture_names()`` / ``cursor.matches()``; the bridge reads ``node.start_byte`` / ``node.end_byte`` / ``node.start_point.{row,column}`` / ``node.end_point.{row,column}`` directly (the same data ``node.range()`` returns) and iterates ``cursor.matches(query, root_node, src)`` -- a real ``tree_sitter.QueryCursor`` / ``Query`` / ``Node`` satisfies this contract; the 17-test suite uses lightweight fakes. Third, **``TYPE_CHECKING`` deferred import breaks the ``scope_graph`` <-> ``languages.types`` cycle** -- ``languages.types`` -> ``scope_graph.nodes`` triggers the ``scope_graph/__init__`` barrel -> ``bridge`` -> ``languages.types`` (partially initialised) -> ``ImportError``; moving ``TSLanguageConfig`` under ``TYPE_CHECKING`` breaks the cycle because ``from __future__ import annotations`` makes annotations lazily-evaluated strings, and the bridge reaches the language config via duck typing (``primary_language_id`` / ``symbol_id_of``) at runtime, never binding the concrete type. Fourth, **barrel extension 16 -> 19** -- grok ``mod.rs`` L13 re-exports the two ``graph.rs`` free functions + L30 inlines ``build_scope_graph``; the port lifts ``build_scope_graph`` / ``extract_symbols_fast`` / ``scope_graph_from_definitions_query`` into ``scope_graph/__init__`` ``__all__`` (3 of the bridge's 4 ``__all__`` symbols; ``range_for_node`` stays bridge-internal as a helper), bringing the surface to 19 -- the SAME contract-evolution pattern R305b (12->15) established (existing barrel tests updated in-place, legitimate evolution not a regression). Fifth, **four free functions, functional clone** -- ``range_for_node`` assembles ``Range``/``Position`` from a node's extents; ``scope_graph_from_definitions_query`` walks matches, classifies captures by dotted name (``name.definition.<sym>`` / ``name.reference.<sym>`` / ``alias.original`` / ``alias.name``), inserts defs into their tightest scope + refs unconditionally, returns ``(graph, alias_pairs)``; ``extract_symbols_fast`` pre-computes ``is_def``/``is_ref`` boolean vectors + alias slot indices so the hot loop does index lookups (NOT per-capture string compares), ~2-3x faster when only the symbol table is needed; ``build_scope_graph`` wraps the pair in ``ScopeGraphResult``.

### Evidence

1. grok ``Range::for_tree_node`` (range.rs L170-L189) -> :func:`range_for_node` -- reads ``node.start_point.row`` / ``column`` / ``start_byte`` + the ``end_`` triple and assembles two ``Position`` objects into a ``Range``. grok goes through ``node.range()``; the bridge reads the direct attributes (the same underlying data) to honour range.py L9-L14's deferred-binding discipline.
2. grok ``scope_graph_from_definitions_query`` (graph.rs L485-L556) -> :func:`scope_graph_from_definitions_query` -- the full parse path. Walks ``cursor.matches(query, root_node, src)``, classifies each capture by ``capture_names[capture.index].split(".")``, buckets def/ref captures, extracts ``(alias_name, original_name)`` pairs, then inserts each def into ``find_tightest_local_scope(range)`` via ``insert_global_def`` and each ref via ``insert_ref_unconditional``. Returns ``(ScopeGraph, list[tuple[str, str]])``.
3. grok ``extract_symbols_fast`` (graph.rs L565-L633) -> :func:`extract_symbols_fast` -- the fast path. Pre-computes ``is_def``/``is_ref`` boolean vectors + ``alias_original_idx``/``alias_name_idx`` slots ONCE before the match loop, so the hot loop does ``is_def[idx]`` index lookups instead of ``capture_name.startswith(...)`` per capture. Collects ``(name, range)`` tuples for defs/refs + ``(alias_name, original_name)`` pairs. ~2-3x faster than the full graph build when only the symbol table is needed.
4. grok ``build_scope_graph`` (mod.rs L30-L38) -> :func:`build_scope_graph` -- thin convenience wrapper that delegates to :func:`scope_graph_from_definitions_query` and wraps the ``(graph, aliases)`` pair in :class:`ScopeGraphResult`.
5. Circular import: ``languages.types`` -> (L46) ``scope_graph.nodes`` -> triggers ``scope_graph/__init__`` barrel -> (L49) ``bridge`` -> (original L41) ``languages.types`` (partially initialised) -> ``ImportError``. Resolved by moving ``TSLanguageConfig`` under ``TYPE_CHECKING``: ``from __future__ import annotations`` makes the annotation a lazily-evaluated string, so the barrel re-export does not bind the concrete type at import time.
6. Duck-typed node contract: ``node.start_byte`` / ``node.end_byte`` / ``node.start_point.{row,column}`` / ``node.end_point.{row,column}`` (read directly by ``range_for_node``); ``capture.node`` + ``capture.index`` (read by both free functions); ``match_.captures`` (iterated); ``cursor.matches(query, root_node, src)`` (the match iteration entry point).
7. Duck-typed query contract: ``query.capture_names`` tolerates BOTH the property form (modern ``tree_sitter.Query.capture_names`` is a ``list``) AND a callable form via :func:`_capture_names` -- the bridge stays binding-version-agnostic.
8. :func:`_new_query_cursor` raises ``RuntimeError`` (NOT ``ImportError``) on missing ``tree_sitter`` -- mirrors R303's ``TSLanguageConfig.language()`` / ``compile_query()`` "bridge needs the binding" signal. Lazy import inside the function body, NOT at module top, so importing ``bridge`` itself never triggers the dependency.
9. Capture-name classification: ``parts = capture_name.split(".")``; ``len == 3 and parts[0] == "name" and parts[1] == "definition"`` -> def bucket (``symbol_id_of(parts[2])``); ``len == 3 and parts[0] == "name" and parts[1] == "reference"`` -> ref bucket; ``parts == ["alias", "original"]`` / ``["alias", "name"]`` -> alias pair. Matches the existing ``TSLanguageConfig`` file-definition query patterns.
10. ``extract_symbols_fast`` signature parity: ``_lang_config`` is accepted (grok takes the language config) but UNUSED -- the fast path classifies captures purely by dotted names, with NO symbol-id resolution; the caller resolves names to symbol ids later via the language config if needed. The leading ``_`` documents the intentional unused parameter.
11. :class:`ScopeGraph` public API consumed by the bridge (all confirmed via the graph-test suite R305b): ``ScopeGraph.new(range, lang)`` / ``find_tightest_local_scope(range) -> LocalScope`` / ``insert_global_def(LocalDef)`` / ``insert_ref_unconditional(Reference)``. The bridge does NOT touch private graph internals.
12. Barrel contract: ``scope_graph/__init__`` ``__all__`` extended 16 -> 19 (3 bridge symbols added alphabetically after ``EdgeKind``: ``build_scope_graph`` / ``extract_symbols_fast`` / ``scope_graph_from_definitions_query``). ``range_for_node`` is deliberately NOT lifted -- it is a bridge-internal helper (no grok ``mod.rs`` re-export counterpart).
13. ``NodeKind.range()`` is a METHOD (not a property) -- the port's tagged-union port returns the scope range for SCOPE/DEF and the identifier range for REF/IMPORT. ``range_for_node`` builds the ``Range`` from a tree-sitter node BEFORE it is wrapped in a ``NodeKind``, so this dispatch does not apply at the bridge seam.

### Round goal

Land direction (2)'s seventh brick: port grok's ``xai-codebase-graph`` crate's ``manager/cache.rs`` (106 lines) to Python under ``minimax_code.xai_codebase_graph.manager.cache``. R305e's roadmap named ``manager/`` (IndexManager + cache serde, consuming R305d's ``save`` / ``load``) the next leaf once the scope_graph parse front closed; R305f narrows to the cache wrapper ONLY -- the thin file-system + error-classification layer that wraps the SGIX binary serialisation landed in R305d (``scope_graph.sgix``). This slice is chosen because it is the SGIX consumption兑现点: R305d shipped the binary envelope as free functions with NO consumer, and R305f is the first caller -- it owns three concerns and nothing else: (1) path derivation (``get_cache_path`` joins a repo root to ``.goto_index.bin``), (2) existence / size probes (``cache_exists`` / ``cache_size``), (3) load / save delegation that re-maps the SGIX tri-state result (``Ok(Some)`` -> value / ``Ok(None)`` -> ``LegacyCacheFormat`` / ``Err`` -> ``CacheIOError``) into a 4-variant exception hierarchy so callers can ``except LegacyCacheFormat`` to trigger a rebuild. The ``manager`` subpackage barrel (``__init__.py``) is created here and re-exports the cache subset only; the ``builder.rs`` / ``lock.rs`` siblings arrive in later bricks. The clone-by-function methodology held: grok's functional contract is preserved verbatim in behaviour (the tri-state result mapping, the fire-and-forget async save, the ``CACHE_FILE_NAME`` constant), while the implementation is Pythonic (an inheritance hierarchy for the error enum, a daemon ``threading.Thread`` for ``std::thread::spawn``, a ``Path`` for ``PathBuf``). This brick CLOSES the SGIX consumption front (R305d's envelope now has a real caller) and OPENS the ``manager/`` subpackage.

### Fusion conclusion

grok's ``cache.rs`` is a 106-line adapter that sits between the on-disk SGIX bytes (R305d) and the future ``IndexManager`` (which decides WHEN to load / save / rebuild). It owns no serialisation logic of its own -- it delegates to ``sgix.save`` / ``sgix.load`` and classifies the result into one of four failure modes so the caller can pattern-match on the rebuild trigger. Six load-bearing facts shape the port. First, **grok's single ``enum CacheError`` with four variants becomes a base + four-subclass inheritance hierarchy, NOT a single class with a ``kind`` field**: grok distinguishes ``IoError`` / ``SerializeError`` / ``DeserializeError`` / ``LegacyFormat`` via enum-variant pattern matching (``match CacheError::LegacyFormat``). Python has no enum-with-payload, and the idiomatic functional clone of a real exception type is one subclass per variant -- ``except CacheError`` catches every variant (mirrors ``Result<T, CacheError>``), while ``except LegacyCacheFormat`` targets the rebuild trigger precisely (mirrors ``match CacheError::LegacyFormat``). A single class with a ``kind`` field would force callers to inspect the field inside the handler, diverging from grok's pattern-match ergonomics. ``CacheIOError`` carries ``.cause`` (the wrapped ``OSError`` / ``struct.error``); ``CacheSerializeError`` / ``CacheDeserializeError`` carry ``.message``; ``LegacyCacheFormat`` carries nothing extra (it is a pure signal). Second, **``save_index_async`` uses a daemon ``threading.Thread``, NOT an asyncio task** -- grok spawns an OS thread (``std::thread::spawn``) so the caller returns immediately while the blocking write happens off-thread. The SGIX write is synchronous blocking I/O (``struct.pack`` + ``file.write``), so an asyncio task would be the WRONG primitive: it would only schedule onto the running loop and STILL block the event thread on the I/O. A real OS thread (via ``threading.Thread``) is the faithful clone -- and ``daemon=True`` makes it die with the interpreter on exit, matching grok's drop-on-process-end behaviour for an orphaned writer thread. Third, **the fire-and-forget contract means the worker SWALLOWS errors and logs** -- grok's ``move ||`` closure body cannot return a ``Result`` to the caller (the caller has already returned), so it logs the failure and exits. The Python port mirrors this: ``_save_index_worker`` wraps ``save_index`` in ``except CacheError`` + ``_logger.warning(...)``; the caller of ``save_index_async`` NEVER sees the failure. Fourth, **the dual-barrel strategy (manager barrel = 12 symbols; crate-root barrel = 8-symbol subset)** -- grok ``manager/mod.rs`` re-exports exactly 8 cache symbols (``CACHE_FILE_NAME`` + ``CacheError`` + 6 functions), and grok ``lib.rs`` L89-L93 re-exports the SAME 8 at the crate root (the crate root never re-exports the enum's variants). The Python port mirrors this topology: ``manager/__init__.py`` re-exports all 12 (the 8 grok symbols + the 4 ``CacheError`` subclasses, because the subclass-per-variant clone needs them reachable at the package surface for ``except LegacyCacheFormat`` arms); the crate-root ``xai_codebase_graph/__init__.py`` re-exports the grok 8-symbol subset ONLY (the 4 subclasses stay ``manager``-subpackage-only, mirroring grok's single enum at the crate root). Fifth, **the ``load_index`` tri-state contract must surface EVERY decode failure as ``CacheIOError``, NOT leak the underlying exception** -- grok funnels every ``io::Error`` through ``?`` into ``CacheError::IoError``, so a caller of ``load_index`` sees ONLY ``CacheError`` variants. The Python ``sgix.read_from`` raises ``ValueError`` (it wraps the raw ``struct.error`` / ``EOFError`` on bad magic / unsupported version / truncated body), so a naive ``except (OSError, struct.error)`` in ``load_index`` would let ``ValueError`` leak -- violating the "only raises ``CacheError``" contract. The port's ``_SGIX_DECODE_ERRORS = (OSError, struct.error, ValueError)`` tuple catches all three so the contract holds; this was surfaced by the truncated-body test (``test_load_index_truncated_body_raises_io_error``) which constructs a valid SGIX header + a promised-but-absent body and asserts ``CacheIOError`` (NOT a leaked ``ValueError``). Sixth, **``Ok(None)`` (legacy magic) maps to ``LegacyCacheFormat``, NOT to a returned ``None``** -- grok's ``load`` returns ``Option<ScopeGraphIndex>`` (``None`` for a non-SGIX file); ``load_index`` translates ``None`` into ``LegacyCacheFormat`` (a raised exception) so the caller's rebuild arm fires. This is the difference between "the cache file is absent / corrupt" (``CacheIOError``) and "the cache file exists but is a legacy format" (``LegacyCacheFormat`` -- rebuild from source). The tri-state (``Ok(Some)`` / ``Ok(None)`` / ``Err``) maps to (return / ``LegacyCacheFormat`` / ``CacheIOError``).

The error-swallow contract (``test_save_index_worker_swallows_cache_error_and_logs``) tests ``_save_index_worker`` SYNCHRONOUSLY (it IS grok's thread body) to avoid a flaky cross-thread ``caplog`` race.

### YAGNI boundaries

- **subclass-per-variant error hierarchy, NOT a ``kind`` field (the functional-clone-of-an-enum boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 1)** -- grok models cache failure as a single ``enum CacheError`` with four variants that callers pattern-match. Python's idiomatic clone of a real exception type is one subclass per variant: ``except CacheError`` catches all (mirrors ``Result<T, CacheError>``); ``except LegacyCacheFormat`` targets the rebuild arm (mirrors ``match CacheError::LegacyFormat``). A single class with a ``kind`` field would force field inspection inside the handler, diverging from grok's pattern-match ergonomics. The 4 subclasses ARE the distinguishable failure modes; they must be reachable at the package surface, which is why the ``manager`` barrel re-exports all 12 while the crate root re-exports only the base + 8 (mirrors grok's single enum at the crate root).
- **daemon ``threading.Thread`` for ``save_index_async``, NOT an asyncio task (the blocking-I/O-off-thread boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 2)** -- grok spawns an OS thread (``std::thread::spawn``) so the caller returns immediately while the blocking write happens off-thread. The SGIX write is synchronous blocking I/O; an asyncio task would schedule onto the running loop and STILL block the event thread on the I/O. A real ``threading.Thread(daemon=True)`` is the faithful clone -- daemon so it dies with the interpreter on exit (matching grok's drop-on-process-end for an orphaned writer). Documented in the ``save_index_async`` docstring.
- **fire-and-forget worker SWALLOWS errors + logs (the detached-thread boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 3)** -- grok's ``move ||`` closure body cannot return a ``Result`` to a caller that has already returned, so it logs + exits. The Python ``_save_index_worker`` mirrors this: ``except CacheError: _logger.warning(...)``; the caller of ``save_index_async`` NEVER sees the failure. The error-swallow test exercises ``_save_index_worker`` SYNCHRONOUSLY (it IS grok's thread body) to avoid a flaky cross-thread ``caplog`` race.
- **dual-barrel strategy (the grok-topology boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 4)** -- grok ``manager/mod.rs`` re-exports 8 cache symbols; grok ``lib.rs`` L89-L93 re-exports the SAME 8 at the crate root. The Python port mirrors this: ``manager/__init__.py`` re-exports 12 (8 grok + 4 subclasses for ``except`` arms); the crate-root barrel re-exports the grok 8 ONLY (subclasses stay subpackage-only, mirroring grok's single enum at the crate root). Lifting the subclasses to the crate root would diverge from grok's public surface.
- **``_SGIX_DECODE_ERRORS`` includes ``ValueError`` (the contract-completeness boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 5)** -- grok funnels every ``io::Error`` through ``?`` into ``CacheError::IoError``, so ``load_index`` only ever raises ``CacheError`` variants. The Python ``sgix.read_from`` raises ``ValueError`` (wrapping ``struct.error`` / ``EOFError``) on bad magic / unsupported version / truncated body; a naive ``(OSError, struct.error)`` tuple would let it leak. The ``(OSError, struct.error, ValueError)`` tuple catches all three so the "only raises ``CacheError``" contract holds. Surfaces via the truncated-body test (valid SGIX header + absent body -> ``CacheIOError``, NOT a leaked ``ValueError``).

## R305g — migrate grok xai-codebase-graph ``manager/builder.rs`` -> ``minimax_code.xai_codebase_graph.manager.builder`` (direction (2) brick 8: IndexBuilder runtime, 1 grok file -> 1 Python module + 2 barrel extensions, ``IndexError`` enum -> ``IndexBuildError`` subclass hierarchy renamed to dodge the Python built-in, dual file-collection ``git ls-files`` -> ``os.walk`` fallback, two-phase parallel ``ThreadPoolExecutor`` orchestration with bounded merge batches, ``process_file_fast`` degrades to ``None`` under missing tree-sitter binding, CLOSES the ``manager`` builder sibling, OPENS the IndexBuilder consumption front)

### Round goal

Land direction (2)'s eighth brick: port grok's ``xai-codebase-graph`` ``manager/builder.rs`` (507 lines) to Python under ``minimax_code.xai_codebase_graph.manager.builder``. R305f's roadmap named ``manager/builder.rs`` (IndexBuilder) the next leaf once the cache wrapper opened the ``manager`` subpackage; R305g delivers the runtime that turns a repo root into a populated ``ScopeGraphIndex``: collect files, parse each via R305e's ``process_file_fast``, and merge the per-file symbol tables in parallel. This slice owns five concerns and nothing else: (1) the ``IndexBuilder`` fluent-config runtime (``with_registry`` classmethod + 5 self-returning setters for threads / gitignore / hidden / chunk / batch); (2) the ``IndexBuildError`` hierarchy (base + 3 subclasses for the walk / thread-panic / I-O failure modes, renamed from grok's ``IndexError`` to avoid shadowing the Python built-in ``IndexError``); (3) dual file collection (``git ls-files`` subprocess with ``os.walk`` fallback -- mirroring grok's ``git2`` + ``ignore::WalkBuilder`` pair); (4) ``process_file_fast`` graceful degradation (returns ``None`` for unsupported / empty / binary / oversized / missing files, AND ``None`` for any language whose tree-sitter binding is absent, so a build never crashes on an unparseable file); (5) two-phase parallel orchestration (``ThreadPoolExecutor`` with bounded merge batches, mirroring grok's rayon ``par_chunks``). The ``manager`` barrel extends 12 -> 17 symbols (5 builder symbols); the crate-root barrel adds ``IndexBuilder`` + ``IndexBuildError`` (mirrors grok ``lib.rs`` re-exporting ``IndexBuilder`` + the ``IndexError`` enum), with the 3 subclasses staying ``manager``-subpackage-only (the SAME asymmetry R305f established for the cache). The clone-by-function methodology held: grok's functional contract is preserved verbatim in behaviour (the dual file-collection strategy, the per-file parse + ordered merge, the parallel chunked batches, the 5MB skip ceiling, the 8KB binary probe), while the implementation is Pythonic (an inheritance hierarchy for the error enum, ``ThreadPoolExecutor`` for rayon, ``subprocess.run`` for ``git2``, ``os.walk`` for ``ignore::WalkBuilder``, the ``IndexBuildError`` rename for the built-in clash). This brick CLOSES the ``manager`` builder sibling and OPENS the IndexBuilder consumption front (the next caller -- ``index_manager.rs`` -- can now drive a full build + cache).

### Fusion conclusion

grok's ``builder.rs`` is a 507-line orchestrator that turns a repository path into a populated ``ScopeGraphIndex``: it decides WHICH files to parse (dual collection), HOW to parse each (delegate to the R305e tree-sitter bridge), and HOW to merge the results (parallel chunks into the shared index). It owns no parsing logic of its own -- it delegates every per-file parse to ``process_file_fast`` (R305e) and classifies failures into one of three modes so the caller can react to a walk failure versus a worker panic. Eight load-bearing facts shape the port. First, **grok's single ``enum IndexError`` with three variants becomes a base + three-subclass inheritance hierarchy, NOT a single class with a ``kind`` field, AND it is RENAMED ``IndexBuildError`` to avoid shadowing the Python built-in ``IndexError``**: grok distinguishes ``Walk`` / ``ThreadPanic`` / ``Io`` via enum-variant pattern matching. Python's idiomatic clone of a real exception type is one subclass per variant -- ``except IndexBuildError`` catches every variant (mirrors ``Result<T, IndexError>``), while ``except IndexWalkError`` targets the collection-phase failure precisely (mirrors ``match IndexError::Walk``). The rename is forced: grok's ``IndexError`` lives in a module namespace so the collision with Python's built-in ``IndexError`` (the sequence-index error) never arises there, but a Python class named ``IndexError`` WOULD shadow the built-in in every module that imports it -- ``IndexBuildError`` preserves the semantic ("an error from building the index") while dodging the shadow. ``IndexWalkError`` / ``IndexThreadPanic`` carry ``.message``; ``IndexIOError`` carries ``.cause`` (the wrapped ``OSError``). Second, **the ``IndexBuilder`` is a fluent-config runtime: ``with_registry`` classmethod + 5 self-returning setters**, mirroring grok's ``IndexBuilder`` struct + ``with_*`` methods. ``with_registry(LanguageRegistry)`` is the entry point (a classmethod alternative-constructor so the common case -- build with a default registry -- is one call); the 5 setters (``with_num_threads`` / ``with_respect_gitignore`` / ``with_skip_hidden`` / ``with_chunk_size`` / ``with_build_batch_size``) each return ``self`` so configuration chains. Third, **dual file collection: ``git ls-files`` subprocess first, ``os.walk`` fallback** -- grok reaches ``git2`` to list tracked files (respecting ``.gitignore`` for free) and falls back to ``ignore::WalkBuilder`` when the repo is not a git worktree. The Python port mirrors this: ``_collect_files_git`` shells out to ``git ls-files`` via ``subprocess.run`` (``check=False`` so a non-zero return -- not a git repo -- returns ``[]`` rather than raising); ``_collect_files_walk`` is the ``os.walk`` fallback that prunes hidden directories (``dirnames[:] = [d for d in dirnames if not d.startswith(".")]``) and always prunes ``.git``. ``_collect_files`` picks git when its output is non-empty, else walks. Fourth, **``process_file_fast`` degrades to ``None`` for FIVE reasons, never raises**: (a) unsupported extension (no language config) -> ``None``; (b) empty file -> ``None``; (c) binary file (the 8KB ``\0`` probe) -> ``None``; (d) oversized file (``> MAX_INDEXABLE_FILE_SIZE = 5MB``) -> ``None``; (e) missing file (``OSError`` on read) -> ``None``. AND a sixth implicit reason: when the tree-sitter binding is absent, ``_get_parser_and_query`` catches ``_TS_BINDING_ERRORS = (ImportError, RuntimeError)`` and returns ``(None, None)``, so ``process_file_fast`` returns ``None`` rather than crashing. This is the load-bearing graceful-degradation decision: a build over a repo with mixed languages MUST NOT crash just because one language's tree-sitter grammar is not installed. Fifth, **the 8KB binary probe (``_BINARY_PROBE_BYTES = 8000``)** -- grok reads the first chunk and checks for a NUL byte to classify a file as binary (skip). The Python port reads the first 8000 bytes and checks for ``\0``; 8000 (not 8192) mirrors grok's constant. Sixth, **``MAX_INDEXABLE_FILE_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024`` (5242880)** -- grok skips files larger than 5MB (a generated / minified / vendored monster would dominate the parse budget). The constant is defined locally in ``builder.py`` (YAGNI: it is not promoted to a shared module until ``index_manager`` lands a second consumer). Seventh, **two-phase parallel orchestration: ``ThreadPoolExecutor`` + bounded merge batches, mirroring grok's rayon ``par_chunks``** -- grok splits the file list into chunks of ``chunk_size``, processes each chunk in parallel on the rayon thread pool, and merges the results into the shared index in bounded ``build_batch_size`` batches (so the merge does not hold the whole repo's symbols in memory at once). The Python port mirrors this: ``ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=num_threads)`` (default ``max(1, cpu_count - 1)``) processes each chunk via ``pool.map(_process_one, batch)``; the per-file results are merged into the index with ordered ``add_definition`` / ``add_reference`` / ``add_alias`` / ``set_file_meta`` calls; ``build_batch_size`` is clamped up to ``chunk_size`` (``build_batch_size = max(build_batch_size, chunk_size)``) so a misconfigured small batch never under-cuts the chunk granularity. The ``_process_one`` closure wraps ``process_file_fast`` in ``try/except Exception`` and re-raises as ``IndexThreadPanic`` so a worker failure surfaces as a build-level exception, not a silent ``None``. Eighth, **the barrel asymmetry mirrors R305f's cache design**: grok ``manager/mod.rs`` re-exports ``IndexBuilder`` + the ``IndexError`` enum, and grok ``lib.rs`` re-exports the SAME ``IndexBuilder`` + ``IndexError`` at the crate root. The Python port mirrors this topology: ``manager/__init__.py`` extends 12 -> 17 (the 5 builder symbols = ``IndexBuilder`` + ``IndexBuildError`` base + 3 subclasses, the subclasses reachable at the package surface for ``except IndexWalkError`` arms); the crate-root barrel adds ``IndexBuilder`` + ``IndexBuildError`` ONLY (the 3 subclasses stay ``manager``-subpackage-only, the SAME asymmetry R305f established for the cache subclasses). Lifting the subclasses to the crate root would diverge from grok's public surface (grok's single enum sits at the crate root; the variants are distinguishable only via pattern match, which in Python means the subclass is the distinguishable failure mode -- but it lives one layer down, mirroring the cache).

### Round goal

Land direction (2)'s ninth brick: port grok's ``xai-codebase-graph`` ``manager/lock.rs`` (539 lines) to Python under ``minimax_code.xai_codebase_graph.manager.lock``. R305g's roadmap named ``manager/lock.rs`` (file lock) the next leaf once the builder sibling landed; R305h delivers the workspace-level locking runtime that coordinates index operations so redundant builds / saves / refreshes do not stomp each other while allowing concurrent readers. This slice owns a single concern -- coordination -- expressed through two layers (mirrors grok's two-layer design): (1) an **in-memory registry** (same-process dedup fast path -- a module-global dict keyed by canonical workspace path tracking shared-reader count vs exclusive-writer flag, guarded by a single :class:`threading.Lock`); (2) **file locks** (cross-process coordination -- an exclusive operation writes a ``.goto_index.lock`` file beside the cache containing ``operation`` / ``pid`` / ``started`` / ``workspace`` lines; a later contender parses it, treats it as stale when the holder PID is dead OR the per-operation timeout elapsed, else backs off). The lock-file format is kept **byte-compatible** with grok so a mixed Rust/Python fleet agrees on liveness. The ``manager`` barrel merge completes here: the 5 lock symbols (:class:`IndexOperation` / :class:`LockResult` / :class:`WorkspaceLockGuard` / :func:`is_operation_in_progress` / :func:`try_lock`) bring ``manager/__init__`` 17 -> 22, and the crate-root barrel adds the same 5 (mirrors grok ``lib.rs`` L89-L93 re-exporting them verbatim -- unlike cache/builder, lock exposes no enum-variant subclasses, so nothing stays ``manager``-subpackage-only and the crate-root surface is byte-identical to grok's). The clone-by-function methodology held: grok's functional contract is preserved verbatim in behaviour (the shared-vs-exclusive mode matrix, the in-memory-then-file two-phase acquire, the rollback-on-file-lock-failure, the stale-timeout reclaim, the RAII release semantics, the byte-compatible file format), while the implementation is Pythonic (:class:`enum.Enum` for the operation enum, a dict+mutex for ``DashMap``, ``release`` + ``__del__`` + ``__enter__``/``__exit__`` for RAII ``Drop``, a single discriminated class for the ``LockResult`` sum type, epoch-second ``int`` for ``SystemTime``/``Duration``, ``Path.resolve`` for ``dunce::canonicalize``, :mod:`logging` for ``tracing``). This brick CLOSES the ``manager`` subpackage (all three siblings -- cache + builder + lock -- now landed and the barrel merged) and OPENS the lock consumption front (the next caller -- ``index_manager.rs`` -- can now drive a build + cache + lock-coordinated refresh).

### Fusion conclusion

grok's ``lock.rs`` is a 539-line coordinator that prevents redundant index operations on the same workspace from stomping each other while permitting concurrent reads. It owns no indexing logic of its own -- it is a pure concurrency primitive consumed by the future ``IndexManager``. Eight load-bearing facts shape the port, all recorded in the ``lock.py`` module docstring's "Functional-clone decisions" list. First, **``enum IndexOperation`` becomes :class:`IndexOperation` (:mod:`enum`), with ``Display`` collapsing to ``__str__`` returning the enum ``value``** -- the enum ``value`` already *is* the lock-file ``operation=`` string (``"load"`` / ``"save"`` / ``"build"`` / ``"background_refresh"``), so a mixed Rust/Python fleet reads identical tokens. The four stale-timeout constants (LOAD/SAVE 120s, BUILD 600s, BG_REFRESH 300s) stay module-private integers compared in seconds via ``stale_timeout()``; they are deliberately NOT hoisted to the crate root (grok ``lib.rs`` does not re-export them). Second, **grok's ``static IN_MEMORY_LOCKS: Lazy<DashMap<PathBuf, InMemoryLockState>>`` becomes a module-global dict behind one :class:`threading.Lock`** -- grok reaches for ``DashMap`` (lock-free concurrent hashmap) because Rust's borrow checker makes a coarse mutex expensive to share across rayon worker threads; Python's GIL plus the tiny/coarse-grained critical sections (a handful of dict reads + writes per acquire) make a single ``threading.Lock`` both correct and simpler than porting a concurrent map. ``once_cell::Lazy`` is unnecessary: the module-level binding initialises at import time. The entry-API atomic check-and-modify that grok performs inside ``DashMap::entry`` becomes a ``with _IN_MEMORY_LOCKS_GUARD:`` block -- same atomicity guarantee (the whole acquire is one critical section), no concurrent readers needed. Third, **RAII ``WorkspaceLockGuard`` + ``Drop`` impl becomes :meth:`release` + ``__del__`` + ``__enter__``/``__exit__``** -- grok's guard releases the lock automatically when it goes out of scope (RAII drop). Python has no RAII, so the port offers THREE release paths: the explicit ``release()`` method, the ``__del__`` destructor (best-effort, mirrors ``Drop`` firing when the binding goes out of scope), and ``__enter__``/``__exit__`` (the Pythonic structured form, ``with guard: ...``). ``release`` is **idempotent** via the ``_released`` flag so all three paths are mutually safe -- ``__del__`` after explicit ``release()`` is a no-op, not a double-release bug. On release the guard (1) decrements/clears the in-memory state, and (2) for exclusive operations only, removes the lock file (tolerating an already-absent file via ``except FileNotFoundError: pass``, matching grok's ``Drop`` swallowing ``NotFound``). Fourth, **grok's ``enum LockResult { Acquired(guard), Busy { operation, holder_pid } }`` becomes a single :class:`LockResult` class with an ``is_acquired`` discriminator** -- Python has no native sum type; two subclasses (``Acquired``/``Busy``) would split ``unwrap``/``release`` logic across classes, while one class with a discriminator keeps them in one place and reads cleaner. :class:`LockResult` also owns the guard's lifetime -- dropping a ``LockResult`` releases the inner guard, exactly as grok's ``LockResult::Acquired(WorkspaceLockGuard)`` drops the guard when the enum value drops. The ``acquired``/``busy`` classmethods mirror grok's enum-variant construction; ``unwrap()`` mirrors grok's ``LockResult::unwrap`` which panics on ``Busy`` (Python raises :class:`RuntimeError` carrying the busy description -- panic has no Python equivalent). Fifth, **``SystemTime`` / ``UNIX_EPOCH`` / ``Duration`` become epoch seconds as :class:`int`** -- grok computes ``age = now.duration_since(started)``; the port computes ``age = _now_epoch() - started`` where ``_now_epoch() = int(time.time())``. Same semantics, one integer subtract, with the ``as_secs`` whole-second granularity grok uses. Sixth, **``is_process_alive`` keeps grok's platform split**: POSIX probes with ``os.kill(pid, 0)`` (``ProcessLookupError`` -> dead, ``PermissionError`` -> alive-but-foreign -- exists but we lack permission to signal it, grok parity, treat as alive); any other ``OSError`` -> dead; non-POSIX returns ``True`` unconditionally and relies on the timeout-based stale path alone. This is grok's deliberate design for non-Unix platforms, preserved faithfully rather than "fixed" -- on Windows the timeout check is the only liveness signal, and that is intentional. Seventh, **``dunce::canonicalize`` becomes :meth:`pathlib.Path.resolve`** (``strict=False`` by default, so a not-yet-existing workspace still canonicalises). ``dunce`` exists in the Rust ecosystem specifically to avoid the UNC ``\\?\`` prefix on Windows; Python's ``resolve`` already returns a usable path without that wart, so no shim is needed. The ``_canonicalize_workspace`` helper wraps ``resolve`` in a belt-and-braces ``except OSError`` fallback to the raw path (grok's ``dunce::canonicalize`` has the same fallback semantics). Eighth, **the cross-process file lock is intentionally NOT an atomic ``O_EXCL`` create** -- grok reads-then-writes with a TOCTOU window (read existing file -> decide stale vs live -> overwrite), and the Python port preserves that faithfulness. The window is benign for this crate's use case (a single agent process per workspace plus rare background refreshes); making it atomic with ``O_EXCL`` would diverge from grok's observable behaviour and break the byte-compatible file-format contract a mixed fleet relies on. The ``_try_acquire_file_lock`` helper embodies this: it parses any existing file, treats it as stale when ``age >= stale_timeout`` OR the holder PID is dead (else returns the blocker's ``(operation_str, pid)``), ensures the parent directory exists (best-effort, mirrors grok), then overwrites with the caller's claim.

### YAGNI boundaries

- **``enum IndexOperation`` -> :class:`Enum` with ``value`` as the lock-file token (the functional-clone-of-an-enum boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 1)** -- grok distinguishes the four operations via enum variants and writes ``as_str()`` to the lock file. Python's :class:`enum.Enum` mirrors this exactly: the variant ``value`` IS the lock-file ``operation=`` string, so ``__str__`` returns ``self.value`` (grok's ``Display`` collapses to ``as_str``). ``is_exclusive()``/``stale_timeout()`` are methods on the enum (grok ``fn`` impls). The 4 stale-timeout constants stay module-private; they are NOT hoisted to the crate root because grok ``lib.rs`` does not re-export them.
- **``DashMap`` in-memory registry -> dict + single :class:`threading.Lock` (the concurrency-primitive boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 2)** -- grok needs ``DashMap`` (lock-free concurrent map) because Rust's borrow checker makes a coarse mutex expensive across rayon workers. Python's GIL + the tiny coarse-grained critical sections (a handful of dict reads/writes per acquire) make a single ``threading.Lock`` both correct and simpler. The atomic ``DashMap::entry`` check-and-mutate becomes one ``with _IN_MEMORY_LOCKS_GUARD:`` block. ``once_cell::Lazy`` is unnecessary: the module-level binding initialises at import time. Documented in the ``lock.py`` module docstring.
- **RAII ``Drop`` -> idempotent ``release`` + ``__del__`` + context-manager (the lifetime boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 3)** -- Python has no RAII, so the port offers THREE release paths (explicit ``release()``, ``__del__`` destructor, ``__enter__``/``__exit__``). The ``_released`` flag makes ``release`` idempotent so all three are mutually safe -- ``__del__`` after explicit release is a no-op, not a double-release bug. ``__del__`` swallows any exception (interpreter-shutdown quirks never leak). Documented in the :class:`WorkspaceLockGuard` docstring.
- **``enum LockResult`` sum type -> single discriminated class (the sum-type-without-a-sum-type boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 4)** -- grok models the acquire outcome as ``enum LockResult { Acquired(guard), Busy { operation, holder_pid } }``. Python has no native sum type; two subclasses would split ``unwrap``/``release`` logic, while one class with an ``is_acquired`` discriminator keeps them in one place. :class:`LockResult` owns the guard's lifetime (dropping the result releases the guard, mirroring grok's ``Acquired`` variant dropping the guard). ``unwrap()`` raises :class:`RuntimeError` on ``Busy`` (grok panics; panic has no Python equivalent). Documented in the :class:`LockResult` docstring.
- **``SystemTime``/``UNIX_EPOCH``/``Duration`` -> epoch-second :class:`int` (the time-representation boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 5)** -- grok computes ``age = now.duration_since(started)``; the port computes ``age = _now_epoch() - started`` where ``_now_epoch() = int(time.time())``. Same semantics, one integer subtract, ``as_secs`` whole-second granularity. No :class:`datetime` overhead (the comparison is a plain int compare).
- **``is_process_alive`` platform split preserved, NOT "fixed" (the platform-parity boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 6)** -- POSIX probes with ``os.kill(pid, 0)`` (``ProcessLookupError`` -> dead, ``PermissionError`` -> alive-but-foreign, other ``OSError`` -> dead); non-POSIX returns ``True`` unconditionally and relies on the timeout check alone. This is grok's deliberate design for non-Unix platforms; making it "better" on Windows would diverge from grok's observable behaviour. The ``test_is_process_alive_dead_pid_posix`` test is the 1 skipped test on Windows -- there is nothing to assert because grok's non-POSIX branch is a constant ``True``.
- **file lock intentionally NOT atomic ``O_EXCL`` (the TOCTOU-parity boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 7)** -- grok reads-then-writes with a TOCTOU window, and the Python port preserves that faithfulness. The window is benign for this crate's use case (single agent per workspace + rare background refreshes); making it atomic would diverge from grok's observable behaviour AND break the byte-compatible file-format contract a mixed Rust/Python fleet relies on. Documented in the ``lock.py`` module docstring (the closing paragraph).
- **``dunce::canonicalize`` -> :meth:`Path.resolve` with no shim (the Windows-UNC boundary -- load-bearing adapter decision 8)** -- ``dunce`` exists in Rust to strip the UNC ``\\?\`` prefix on Windows; Python's ``resolve`` already returns a usable path without that wart, so no shim is needed. ``_canonicalize_workspace`` wraps ``resolve`` in a belt-and-braces ``except OSError`` fallback to the raw path (grok's ``dunce::canonicalize`` has the same fallback).
- **crate-root barrel byte-identical to grok (the grok-topology boundary)** -- grok ``lib.rs`` L89-L93 re-exports the 5 lock symbols verbatim. Unlike cache (4 subclasses) and builder (3 subclasses), lock exposes NO enum-variant subclasses (the ``LockResult`` sum type collapsed to a single class, and ``IndexOperation`` is a plain enum), so nothing stays ``manager``-subpackage-only -- the crate-root surface is byte-identical to grok's, not a subset. The 4 stale-timeout constants stay leaf-only (grok does not re-export them).
- **POSIX-only liveness test skipped on Windows (the platform-test-isolation boundary)** -- ``test_is_process_alive_dead_pid_posix`` is ``pytest.skip``-guarded on non-POSIX (grok's non-POSIX ``is_process_alive`` is a constant ``True``, so the dead-PID assertion cannot run). This is the +1 in the skipped count (14 -> 15); it is NOT a regression -- it is a faithful, platform-correct test that simply has no assertion to make on Windows.
- **transient timing-flaky ``test_connection`` NOT fixed (iteration-independence boundary, continues R298/.../R305g)** -- ``test_connection.py::test_interval_keeps_global_timeline_across_loops`` is a wall-clock precision assertion; its occasional failure is machine-load-sensitive. It STABLE-PASSED R305h's regression run but remains a known flake; per the iteration-independence rule it is NOT fixed in R305h (no ``xai_codebase_graph`` code in the connection suite).
- **Revised roadmap**: R305h (this) CLOSES the ``manager`` subpackage barrel merge -- all three siblings (cache + builder + lock) are now landed and the ``manager/__init__`` barrel reaches its final 22-symbol shape (mirrors grok ``manager/mod.rs``). Next leaves: ``index_manager.rs`` (2185 lines, where the duplicate ``index_manager::FileEvent`` is published -- the first real consumer of the full ``manager`` surface: cache + builder + lock coordinated) -> ``navigation.rs`` (844 lines, where the duplicate ``navigation::Location`` is published). Direction (3) L2 self-evolution framework skeleton wiring remains P0 not-started parallel active front.

`feat(platform): R305h port manager/lock.rs -> lock.py (workspace locking + IndexOperation enum + DashMap->dict+Lock + RAII release + LockResult discriminated class + stale-takeover + barrel merge)` (feat commit, 5 files: 1 new [manager/lock.py 654 lines] + 1 new test [its 36-function/41-item suite, 552 lines] + 2 barrel extensions [manager/__init__ 17 -> 22 + crate-root __init__ adds the 5 lock symbols] + 1 barrel-test update [builder suite: 17-symbol assertion -> 22-symbol, the R305h barrel extension is in-scope]). feat commit: the workspace-level locking runtime -- porting grok ``manager/lock.rs`` (539 lines), the concurrency primitive that coordinates index operations so redundant builds/saves/refreshes do not stomp each other while allowing concurrent readers. Owns one concern -- coordination -- through two layers: (1) in-memory registry (same-process dedup fast path); (2) file locks (cross-process coordination with byte-compatible format). The LOAD-BEARING decision is functional-clone, NOT line-clone, surfaced through EIGHT adapter decisions: (1) ``enum IndexOperation`` -> :class:`Enum` [the variant ``value`` IS the lock-file ``operation=`` string so ``__str__`` returns ``self.value`` mirroring grok ``Display``->``as_str``; ``is_exclusive``/``stale_timeout`` are enum methods; the 4 stale-timeout constants stay module-private, NOT hoisted to crate root mirroring grok ``lib.rs``]; (2) ``DashMap`` -> dict + :class:`threading.Lock` [grok needs lock-free concurrent map for rayon workers under the borrow checker; (3) RAII ``Drop`` -> idempotent ``release`` + ``__del__`` + context-manager [Python has no RAII so the port offers THREE release paths; ``_released`` flag makes them mutually safe -- ``__del__`` after explicit release is a no-op not a double-release bug; ``__del__`` swallows any exception so shutdown quirks never leak]; (4) ``enum LockResult`` sum type -> single discriminated class [Python has no native sum type; two subclasses would split ``unwrap``/``release`` logic, one class with ``is_acquired`` discriminator keeps them together; the class owns the guard's lifetime mirroring grok's ``Acquired`` variant dropping the guard; ``unwrap()`` raises :class:`RuntimeError` on ``Busy`` mirroring grok panic]; (5) ``SystemTime``/``Duration`` -> epoch-second :class:`int` [``age = _now_epoch() - started`` with ``int(time.time())``; same semantics one int subtract, ``as_secs`` granularity]; (6) ``is_process_alive`` platform split preserved NOT fixed [POSIX ``os.kill(pid,0)`` with ``ProcessLookupError``->dead/``PermissionError``->alive-but-foreign/other-``OSError``->dead; non-POSIX returns ``True`` unconditionally relying on timeout alone -- grok's deliberate design for non-Unix]; (7) file lock intentionally NOT atomic ``O_EXCL`` [grok reads-then-writes with a TOCTOU window, port preserves that faithfulness; the window is benign for single-agent-per-workspace use; making it atomic would diverge from grok AND break the byte-compatible file-format contract]; (8) ``dunce::canonicalize`` -> :meth:`Path.resolve` [``dunce`` exists to strip the UNC ``\\?\`` prefix; Python ``resolve`` already returns a usable path, no shim needed; belt-and-braces ``except OSError`` fallback to raw path]. Non-obvious discovery 1: the file-lock-contested rollback is LOAD-BEARING -- when ``_try_acquire_file_lock`` reports a live contender, ``try_lock`` MUST call ``_release_in_memory_lock`` before returning ``Busy``, otherwise the workspace stays exclusive-locked in memory (the in-memory acquire succeeded in step 1) and a subsequent shared ``Load`` would be blocked forever by a phantom exclusive flag; ``test_file_lock_contested_releases_in_memory`` locks this by planting a live lock file, asserting ``busy_operation == "build"`` (from the file, proving the file stage was reached AFTER the in-memory acquire), then asserting a subsequent ``Load`` succeeds (proving rollback). Non-obvious discovery 2: the ``LockResult`` single-class discriminator is NOT a compromise vs two subclasses -- it is the cleaner choice because ``unwrap``/``release``/``__del__``/``__enter__``/``__exit__`` all stay in one place, and the class owning the guard's lifetime (dropping the result releases the guard) is a natural fit for Python's lack of move semantics. Non-obvious discovery 3: the POSIX-only ``test_is_process_alive_dead_pid_posix`` is the +1 in the skipped count (14 -> 15), NOT a regression -- it is ``pytest.skip``-guarded on non-POSIX because grok's non-POSIX ``is_process_alive`` is a constant ``True`` and there is simply no dead-PID assertion to make on Windows; the test exists to lock the POSIX branch where it CAN run. Non-obvious discovery 4: the crate-root barrel is byte-identical to grok's, NOT a subset like cache/builder -- because the ``LockResult`` sum type collapsed to a single class and ``IndexOperation`` is a plain enum, there are NO enum-variant subclasses to keep ``manager``-subpackage-only; the 4 stale-timeout constants are the only leaf-only symbols (grok does not re-export them).
